chapter: Climax Rag and tempo and meter
title: Jim Robinson's trombone part on Climax Rag
summary: On the second reel, DeVore tells how Jim Robinson, after a Sunday session on July 1, sang the missing trombone part of Climax Rag to Rusty; they mention the earlier record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: This is rail 3 of Charlie DeVore. July 4, 1962 it is.

Yeah, well I want to just talk a little bit about the individual instruction from the New Orleans guys. Now, we had a session Sunday afternoon, which is the 1st of July, and we played a tune called Climax Rag, which is quite popular with Percy and George Lewis's band played a little bit. And Jim likes that tune a lot, and after when we got through... Howard too. Oh yeah, Howard plays it great. He plays all his own stuff in there. But afterwards Jim came up to me and said, hey I heard it. You know how Jim stutters and everything. What are you saying man? Yeah. What's best?

Yeah, that's it. He said, man I heard that Climax Rag, you know. He says, you like that tune. And he said, we played it all the time. He said, I heard you steal that from me. That's what he said anyway. But he said, it's a trombone partner that you didn't play. And he was talking to a trombone man. And he sang it to him, see. And Rusty didn't get it the first time around. He's like me, it takes about 20 times around and doesn't really get it. But then once he gets it, he usually remembers it. And it's things like that that you can pick up on an individual basis. Where you hear a tune and maybe there's a real way of doing it that to do it this way, you're not exactly copying. If you didn't do it this way, it wouldn't be really the tune, you see. And Jim had that trombone part that he was singing to Rust. I've heard him do it on the records and it's on there every time. And you see, Rust didn't do it when we were playing it. So Jim thought that he would show them and sing it to him. So he'd pick it up so we'd play. He said, that's part of the tune. And the last night we were talking about it. And he said, well, there's not too much for a trombone to do on that. In a way something's really distinctly trombone. Jim wasn't, yeah, you know how Jim talks. But that's what he was getting at. And so when you come up with something like that, it's nice to play those things. And he went over it with Rust and sang it a couple of times. And I remember, as soon as he started singing it, I remember having heard it on Bill's, the climax sessions at the tea room. And then, I don't know, I told Jim that I thought he played it great on the Hup record, but nobody's heard the Hup record down here.
It was down here but not much. Yeah. I know.
You have it. Yeah, that's uh, that's a... That's a... That's a Swans catalog.
I thought they cut it off.
This wasn't some guy in Florida. Well, he was on the Hup. Jim couldn't remember the Hup session at all. Well, that's 12 years ago. Yeah. Oh yeah, absolutely.
Well, not only that, he probably didn't know it was being recorded.
Yeah, I think that was the date.
Yeah, it was made at a concert.

Yeah. Auditorium, yeah. So he pointed that out, you know. And like on Climax Ragnar, you've got to play it that way. And if you take the sheet music, I heard a piano transcription of that tune and listened to the melody on there and followed that real close. But you see, a New Orleans guy wouldn't do it exactly the way it was written. And that's what a young guy could pick up individually.
